title: The Driftwood Tower at Tybee Point

passage.title: The Driftwood Tower at Tybee Point
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Salt wind whipped across the wide sandbar at the north end of Tybee Island. Twelve-year-old Caleb shaded his eyes and looked down the beach toward the distant wooden pier. His aunt and uncle had promised to paddle their yellow kayaks around the point at four o'clock. Low dunes and tall sea oats blocked the family camp from the open water. Caleb and his cousin Nora wanted to build a tall driftwood marker so the paddlers could spot their landing zone from far out at sea.

Time was running short because the afternoon tide had already started to creep up the slope. Foamy waves hissed across the flat shells and crept closer to the dry sand every minute. If the cousins built their tower too low on the beach, the rising surf would knock the whole frame down. They scrambled along the high tide line to gather gray cedar limbs bleached white by the sun. Nora dragged three thick poles to the top of a firm shell mound above the water mark.

At first, Caleb tried to prop the three tall poles together like a simple tent. As soon as he let go, a sharp gust off the ocean blew the loose wood flat into the sand. He realized that smooth driftwood needed a deep anchor and strong ties to survive the coastal breeze. Using a curved clam shell, he dug three deep holes into the damp sand at the base of the mound. Once the heavy ends were buried two feet deep, the frame stood steady.

Next, the cousins searched the wrack line for dried marsh vines to lash the top joints together. The longest cedar branch, crowned with a bright red towel that fluttered like a lighthouse flag, was firmly braced by Nora between the upright posts. She wrapped the tough vines around the crossed wood until the center pole could not wobble. Even when a strong gust rattled the sea oats, the five-foot tower held its ground.

Just as Nora tied the final knot, two bright yellow kayaks glided around the rocky jetty. Half a mile out, Uncle Devon raised his double paddle high in the air to wave at the red flag. Without that tall beacon on the shell mound, the paddlers might have drifted past the camp toward the marsh. Caleb grinned and brushed the wet sand from his knees as the kayaks turned toward shore. Working together with smart planning had beaten both the wind and the rising tide.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"The longest cedar branch, crowned with a bright red towel that fluttered like a lighthouse flag, was firmly braced by Nora between the upright posts."

Based on the way this sentence is written, who or what braced the cedar branch?

options.text: The bright red towel braced Nora against the ocean wind.
options.childFeedback: This mixes up the sentence parts! The bright red towel was tied to the top of the branch as a flag; it did not brace Nora.

options.text: The lighthouse flag braced the upright posts in the wet sand.
options.childFeedback: The red towel only fluttered like a lighthouse flag on top of the branch—Nora is the one who braced the wood between the posts.

options.text: Nora braced the longest cedar branch between the upright posts.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, the phrase 'by Nora' right after 'was firmly braced' tells us that Nora is the person who braced the longest cedar branch between the upright posts.

options.text: Uncle Devon braced the cedar branch using his yellow kayak paddle.
options.childFeedback: Uncle Devon was still paddling his kayak out on the water in Paragraph 4 and did not help build the driftwood tower on shore.

questions.provingSentenceText: The longest cedar branch, crowned with a bright red towel that fluttered like a lighthouse flag, was firmly braced by Nora between the upright posts.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, the phrase 'by Nora' right after 'was firmly braced' tells us that Nora is the person who braced the longest cedar branch between the upright posts.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'The longest cedar branch' is the subject receiving the action, while the prepositional phrase 'by Nora' identifies Nora as the person who braced it.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words 'was firmly braced by Nora' in Paragraph 4 to see who is doing the bracing.

questions.prompt:

"Half a mile out, Uncle Devon raised his double paddle high in the air to wave at the red flag. Without that tall beacon on the shell mound, the paddlers might have drifted past the camp toward the marsh."

What does the word beacon mean as it is used in Paragraph 5?

options.text: A guiding signal that can be seen from far away
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, 'beacon' means a guiding signal that can be seen from far away, because the tall red-flagged tower helped the kayakers spot the camp from half a mile out.

options.text: A sharp shell used for digging deep holes in sand
options.childFeedback: Caleb used a curved clam shell to dig holes back in Paragraph 3, but in Paragraph 5 the 'tall beacon on the shell mound' refers to the signal tower.

options.text: A strong ocean current that pushes boats toward a marsh
options.childFeedback: A current pushes boats in the water, whereas the tall beacon stood on top of the shell mound to keep the paddlers from drifting past the camp.

options.text: A wooden kayak paddle painted bright yellow
options.childFeedback: Uncle Devon waved his yellow paddle when he saw the red flag, so the beacon on the shell mound was the tower on shore, not his paddle.

questions.provingSentenceText: Without that tall beacon on the shell mound, the paddlers might have drifted past the camp toward the marsh.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, 'beacon' means a guiding signal that can be seen from far away, because the tall red-flagged tower helped the kayakers spot the camp from half a mile out.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 5, 'that tall beacon' refers back to the five-foot driftwood tower topped with a red flag that guided the kayakers to their landing spot from half a mile away.

options.text: All of the dried marsh vines grow only on top of the rocky jetty.

options.text: They want to keep the rising tide from knocking their driftwood frame down.

questions.prompt: How does the failure of Caleb's first tower in Paragraph 3 move the plot forward?

options.text: It causes the cousins to give up on building and swim out to meet the kayaks instead.
options.childFeedback: Caleb and Nora never give up or swim out to the kayaks; instead, they fix the design by digging deep holes and tying the joints with vines.

options.text: It leads Caleb to dig deep anchor holes so the poles can stand firm against the wind.
options.childFeedback: When the ocean gust blows down the loosely propped poles in Paragraph 3, Caleb realizes the tower needs deep anchor holes and strong ties, leading him to bury the posts two feet deep.

options.text: It shows that the wind is too strong for anyone to paddle a kayak around Tybee Point.
options.childFeedback: Although the coastal breeze knocks over the loose poles at first, the aunt and uncle still paddle their kayaks safely around the point in Paragraph 5.

options.text: It explains why the cedar limbs had turned white from lying in the bright sun.
options.childFeedback: The sun-bleached cedar limbs were already mentioned in Paragraph 2; the collapse in Paragraph 3 shows why the poles needed deep anchors in the sand.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the story?

options.text: Kayakers should always carry a radio instead of looking for landmarks on the shore.
options.childFeedback: Radios are never mentioned in the passage, and the driftwood landmark on the shore worked well to guide the kayakers home.

options.text: Ocean beaches are too windy for building anything out of natural driftwood.
options.childFeedback: The cousins successfully build a sturdy five-foot driftwood tower that holds its ground against the gusts, proving beaches are not too windy to build on.

options.text: Careful planning and teamwork can overcome natural challenges when a first attempt fails.
options.childFeedback: The story shows how Caleb and Nora overcome the rising tide and strong wind after their first tower falls by working together and planning a stronger anchored design.

options.text: Clam shells are better digging tools than metal shovels on a sandy island.
options.childFeedback: Metal shovels are never compared to clam shells in the story, and using a shell to dig is just one small detail rather than the central theme.

questions.provingSentenceText: Working together with smart planning had beaten both the wind and the rising tide.
questions.childTip: The story shows how Caleb and Nora overcome the rising tide and strong wind after their first tower falls by working together and planning a stronger anchored design.
questions.parentExplanation: Throughout the story, Caleb and Nora adapt their plan (choosing high ground, digging anchor holes, lashing with vines) and work together to beat the wind and tide.
questions.retryHint: Look at the final sentence of Paragraph 5 to see what lesson Caleb and Nora's success teaches about teamwork and planning.
